headline: 5.8-Degree Break at 39°20'N Holding Yellowfin on the Canyon's East Wall
subhead: The warm filament we flagged last week never slid off — it's still parked over the Hudson, and the tuna know exactly where the edge is.
body_markdown:
5.8 degrees. That's the spread I marked yesterday running the SST overlay before first light — 79.4°F on the blue water side of the filament, down to 73.6°F where it meets the canyon's cooler upwelling near the 100-fathom curve. That's about as clean a break as you'll find on the Hudson all season, and it's sitting almost exactly where I said it would last week when the winds stayed offshore and stable. We flagged that the pattern would hold as long as the edge water didn't cool off — and it hasn't. The filament's still parked over the canyon, running roughly east-northeast from 39°22'N, 72°48'W down through 39°10'N, 72°28'W, which puts the hottest push of water right over the Dip and spilling out toward the Claw.

That break is doing exactly what it's supposed to do — pushing bait up out of 900 to 1,400 feet of water and stacking it against the thermal wall where the yellowfin are working. Boats running out of Manasquan and Shark River have been putting spreads out starting around the 100-fathom line, working east along the color change — you can see it if you're paying attention, a hard line between green-blue chlorophyll-rich water inshore and that gin-clear cobalt on the canyon side, chlorophyll readings dropping under 0.3 mg/m³ once you cross it. Ballyhoo skirted in pink/white and green machine combos, run 30 to 40 feet back off the shotgun and riggers, have been drawing strikes consistently once boats hit that edge. Cedar plugs and small Zucchi-style trolling lures in the pattern have also been picking off fish in the 40 to 60-pound range on the troll, especially in that 8 AM to 11 AM window before the wind fills in.

Bigeye have been showing on the meter holding deep during daylight, sitting tight to bottom structure in the 900 to 1,100-foot range along the canyon wall near the Claw — no surprise there, that's textbook daytime behavior for them, hugging the thermocline where the water's stable and dark. Guys running deep drops with squid strips and glow beads on 200-pound fluorocarbon leaders have connected after dark on drift, working the same real estate the daytime bigeye vacate once the sun goes down and they come up to feed in that 400 to 600-foot band.

Mahi have been mixed in wherever there's floating structure — pushed-up weed lines were showing thicker than I've seen in a couple weeks, probably a byproduct of that same warm filament dragging Sargasso mats up from the south. Most of what we're seeing is schoolie-sized, 3 to 8 pounds, but there've been a few gaffer-class fish in the 12 to 15-pound range holding under the bigger mats out past the Dip. Small chartreuse and pink squid daisy chains worked slow past the weed edges have been the ticket, and it's worth a few minutes with lightweight spinning gear and a chunk of butterfish once you spot color under the mat — that's usually where the bigger ones are hanging.

White marlin sightings have picked up too, though it's been more teaser strikes than actual releases — a handful of boats out of Brielle and Point Pleasant have had multiple shots on dink ballyhoo and green machine teaser combos worked off the outriggers, but conversion's been spotty. That's typical for early August before the fish really commit — the water's right, the bait's right, but they're still testing the spread more than eating it. If you're marlin-focused, I'd stack more dink baits and less hardware, and keep someone on the pitch rod at all times.

Wahoo have been a bycatch story more than a target — a couple fish in the 30 to 45-pound range came off high-speed spreads run just inside the break itself, where the current shear tends to hold them. If you're not specifically rigged for wahoo with wire leader in the mix, don't be shocked if you get bit off — worth running at least one or two wire-leadered lures if you're covering that edge water seriously.

Honest read on the week: it's been good, not great. Three trips I know of personally connected on all three, but fish counts were modest — four to seven yellowfin per boat, one or two bigeye on the overnight drift, mahi filling in the gaps. This isn't a wide-open bite where you just point the boat and troll — you need to find that exact break, and it's moved a few miles east since Monday as the eddy shifts. Bring patience and a good chart.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward new phase over the next several days, which should tighten up current on the canyon edge and could sharpen the bite window in the early morning hours. If the filament holds its current position — and there's no sign in the chlorophyll or SST data of it sliding off yet — I'd expect the pattern to stay consistent through the weekend. The one thing to watch is any cooling trend on the edge water; if that break narrows below 4 degrees, that's your signal the warm water's starting to lose its grip on the canyon, and you'll need to run farther east to stay on fish. For now, I'd set up on that 39°20'N line and work the color change methodically — that's where I'm putting my program this week.
